entries.label: Baking day
entries.text:
A note of the bread notes, an example of the wiki add-on. One term is defined
in a heading, by the paragraph after it; the note links to the other notes' sections, and its
:term[…] uses to the glossary.
An hour before the loaf comes out of the fridge, after the proof,
the Dutch oven goes into the oven at 250°C, lid on.

entries.label: Scoring
entries.text:
Scoring is cutting the top of the loaf just before it goes in, so that it opens where you
choose instead of tearing at its weakest point.
One long cut a few millimetres deep, with a razor blade held at a low angle, gives an ear: a
flap of crust that lifts and browns.

entries.label: Steam and oven spring
entries.text:
Oven spring is the loaf's last rise, in the first minutes of baking, as the gas in it
expands and the yeast has a final burst before the heat kills it.
It needs a moist surface: under the lid, the loaf's own steam keeps the crust soft long enough
to stretch.
20 minutes at 250°C with the lid on.
25 minutes at 230°C with it off, until the crust is a deep brown and the base sounds hollow
when tapped.
A loaf that springs little was usually over-proofed (the poke test
says when) or shaped too loosely.

entries.label: The crumb
entries.text:
The inside of the loaf: the bread around its holes.
An even, open crumb with a shine on the walls of its holes comes of a good
bulk fermentation; big holes under the crust over dense bread mean it was cut short. A
higher hydration opens it up too.
Let the loaf cool for an hour before cutting it: the crumb is still setting, and cut warm it
turns gummy.

entries.label: Bulk fermentation and the proof
entries.text:
A note of the bread notes, an example of the wiki add-on. One term is defined
by a :dfn[…] with title=, its canonical form; the :term[…] uses name terms the other
notes define, one of them inflected, and link to the glossary.

entries.label: Bulk fermentation
entries.text:
The bulk fermentation is the dough's first rise, in one piece, from mixing in the
levain to shaping.
It takes four to six hours at 24°C, longer in a cool kitchen:
Every 30 minutes for the first two hours, a set of folds: lift one side of the dough, fold
it over, turn the bowl, four times round.
Then leave it alone until it has grown by half, is domed at the edges and shows bubbles on
the sides of the bowl.
The clock matters less than the dough. A dough at a high hydration needs more folds,
and a gentler hand at the end.

entries.label: Shaping
entries.text:
Turn the dough out, pre-shape it into a loose round and let it rest for 20 minutes. Then shape
it tight: the tension of its surface holds it up in the oven. It goes into a floured basket,
seam side up.

entries.label: The proof
entries.text:
Proofing is the last rise, in the shape the loaf will bake in.
Mine is in the fridge overnight, 12 to 16 hours at 4°C. The cold slows the yeast more than
the bacteria, so the bread tastes more sour, and a cold dough is easier to
score.
The poke test says when it is ready: a floured finger pressed in leaves a dent that springs
back slowly, halfway. A dent that springs back at once wants more time; one that stays is
over-proofed, and the loaf will spread in the oven. It is still worth baking: flatter, with a
closer crumb, and as good toasted.

entries.text:
The glossary of the bread notes, an example of the wiki add-on: ::glossary

each linked to its definition and shown as it reads there. A :term[…] in a note links to

entries.label: Hydration and baker's percentages
entries.text:
A note of the bread notes, an example of the wiki add-on. A titled
:::definition block defines its title, a :dfn[…] the word in its sentence; the
:term[…] uses name terms the other notes define, and link to the glossary.
Bakers write a recipe against its flour, so that it scales by a single number.

entries.label: definition
entries.title: Baker's percentage
entries.text:
An ingredient's weight as a share of the flour's, which counts as 100%: 750 g of water to
1000 g of flour is 75%.

entries.label: Hydration
entries.text:
A dough's hydration is its water as a baker's percentage of its flour. The levain
counts too, since it is half flour and half water.
65 to 70% holds its shape on the bench and is easy to handle; the crumb is
tighter.
75 to 80% is slack and sticky, with a more open crumb and a thinner crust.
Over 80% wants strong flour and practice: wet hands, and folds instead of kneading.
Wholemeal flour drinks more water than white: add about 5% for every 20% of wholemeal in the
flour.

entries.label: My everyday loaf
entries.text:
Ingredient
Weight
Baker's %
White bread flour
900 g
90%
Wholemeal rye
100 g
10%
Water
720 g
72%
Levain
200 g
20%
Salt
20 g
2%
With the levain's 100 g of flour and 100 g of water, the whole dough is
\frac{720 + 100}{1000 + 100} \approx 75\% water.

entries.label: Autolyse
entries.text:
An  autolyse  is a rest of the flour and the water alone, before the levain
and the salt go in. Half an hour is enough for the flour to take up the water: the dough comes
together with less kneading and stretches further. I hold back 20 g of the water and add it
with the salt and the levain, at the start of the bulk fermentation.

entries.label: Bread notes
entries.text:
An example of the wiki add-on: a folder of notes as a
wiki. This front page searches the notes with ::search and lists them with ::notes; the
notes define their terms with :dfn[…] and link to them with :term[…], and
the glossary gathers them with ::glossary. All three read the files
luccet index wrote beside the notes. The page loads ../notes.js and ../search.js, this
repository's copies, and the classic theme.
What I have learned baking sourdough at home, a note for each stage, from the jar in the fridge
to a loaf cooling on the rack. A word with a dotted underline links to its entry in
the glossary.

entries.label: Keeping a starter
entries.text:
A note of the bread notes, an example of the wiki add-on. It defines its terms
with :dfn[…], one of them inside :definition[…] because its paragraph goes on, and uses
:term[…] for one that another note defines; each use links to the glossary.
A starter is a culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria, kept alive in flour and
water.
Mine lives in a jar in the fridge and has been going since March.

entries.label: Feeding
entries.text:
Once a week, and the day before a bake:
Keep 20 g of the old starter and throw the rest away.
Add 100 g of flour, four parts white to one part wholemeal rye, and 100 g of water at about
26°C: a starter at 100% hydration.
Mark the level on the jar with a rubber band and leave it out.
It is ready when it has doubled and its top is domed, four to six hours later in a warm
kitchen. A starter that has peaked and fallen back smells sharp, of vinegar, and is better fed
again before it is used.

entries.label: The levain
entries.text:
A  levain  is a portion of the starter, fed for one bake and used up in it.
I build mine the evening before, from 20 g of starter, 100 g of flour and 100 g of water; by
morning it is the 200 g that my everyday loaf takes, and a little
over. The jar goes back in the fridge untouched.
A separate levain leaves the starter on its own schedule: a bake that goes wrong costs a
levain, not the culture.

entries.label: When it is sluggish
entries.text:
Feed it twice a day for two days, at room temperature.
Use more rye: it ferments faster than white flour.
Mind the water: chlorine slows the culture, and tap water left to stand overnight has lost
most of it.
